chat_messages.text:
Great question, and you've identified the most important tension in the spec.

**What "project workspace" actually means**

It's just a structured web UI. Think of it as phases laid out like cards — you click into a phase, it shows you what to learn, what to build, which tasks are AI-appropriate vs human-required, and a chat interface for the gate conversation. That's it. No code, no files, no terminal. It's closer to a Notion page with a built-in chatbot than anything resembling an IDE.

**How the gate works without seeing code — and why it's a real weakness**

This is the honest answer: it can't verify the code. The spec admits this directly. That's why the anchor statement exists — before Turn 1 the user writes one sentence describing what they built and names a specific variable or function. The gate then interrogates them about that self-reported detail. But the spec explicitly calls this out as the MVP's biggest weakness:

"The anchor statement is self-reported and unverified. A student could fabricate a variable name."

The structural defense is that by Turn 3 the hypothetical is so specific to their claimed implementation that fabricating consistently across all three turns becomes as much work as just understanding it. It's friction, not verification. It's not foolproof and the spec doesn't claim it is.

**The v2 solution the spec points to**

Code submission. The user pastes their code or connects their GitHub repo via OAuth, Codize can actually read the files, and the gate questions are generated from real variable names, real functions, real architectural decisions it can see. That makes the anchor statement verifiable, the hypotheticals more precise, and cheating significantly harder. That's why GitHub OAuth is probably the single most important v2 feature — it's not just convenience, it closes the fundamental integrity gap in the gate.

So right now Codize is essentially running on the honor system with enough friction to make cheating inconvenient. The real version of Codize, the one where the gate is genuinely trustworthy, requires seeing the code.

chat_messages.text:
Based on the spec's in-scope list, here's exactly what exists by October 26.

**What a user actually experiences**

They sign up, and immediately — no homepage, no dashboard — they get the first intake question. Five conversational questions later, Codize classifies their project and generates a phase-by-phase roadmap. They see something like 8-10 phase cards with titles, concept summaries, and a timeline. They click Phase 1, read the concept explanation written specifically for their project, see the task list split into AI-appropriate and human-required columns, and go work in their own editor.

They come back, open the gate, write one sentence describing what they built naming a specific variable or function, and have a 3-turn conversation with Codize about their actual implementation decisions. Pass it and Phase 2 unlocks. Fail it and they wait 30 minutes. At some point unexpectedly a functional unlock appears — a pre-built component drops in that saves them real setup time.

If they disappear for 3 days and come back, before they can access anything a modal appears with their exact purpose statement from intake in large text and a single button that says "Let's keep building."

That's the full loop.

**What it looks like visually**

Three screens. The spec is explicit about this.

Screen 1 is the intake conversation — just a chat interface, one question at a time, no form.

Screen 2 is the roadmap — phase cards, clickable, showing progress. Probably the least designed thing in the app since the spec says rough is fine.

Screen 3 is the phase workspace — concept explanation on one side, task list with AI/human labels, and the gate chat interface at the bottom.

Desktop only. No mobile. The spec says rough and functional is the standard — no design polish until the core loop works.

**What it is NOT by October**

No code editor. No GitHub connection. No way for Codize to see their actual code. No mobile. No payments. No social features. No fourth archetype. The gate only has Option A — the architecture explanation path. Option B, the bug hunt, requires seeing code so it doesn't exist yet.

**The honest version**

By October you have a working proof of concept that demonstrates the core loop convincingly to anyone who uses it. It won't look impressive from the outside — three rough screens, desktop only, three project types. But if the gate actually works and holds up under real usage, you have something genuinely novel that you built and can defend completely in an interview, which is exactly what the project is supposed to teach you to do.

The most impressive thing about the October version won't be the UI. It'll be that you can open the eval results, show 93% Socratic compliance, point to the fix log showing you found a failure and improved it, and explain every architectural decision from the RLS policies to the gate evaluator prompt. That's what makes it stand out.

chat_messages.text:
Yes, but they're very different bets. Let me be direct about each.

**VS Code Extension**

This is the highest impact thing you could eventually build, and here's why — it eliminates the biggest UX friction in the entire product. Right now the user has to context switch constantly. They're coding in VS Code, they hit a phase task, they alt-tab to Codize in the browser, they do the gate conversation, they alt-tab back. That context switching is annoying and every annoying thing in a learning tool accelerates dropout.

A VS Code extension means Codize lives in a sidebar while they code. The gate conversation happens right there. The phase tasks are visible while they're looking at the actual code. And critically — the extension can see the files they have open, which means it could read their code directly and close the gate integrity gap without needing GitHub OAuth at all.

The problem is it's a completely separate technical foundation like the spec says. VS Code extensions are TypeScript, they have their own API, their own deployment pipeline through the VS Code marketplace. It's not something you bolt on — it's essentially a second client for your backend. Realistically that's a post-October project, probably early 2027 if you stay on track.

**Bring Your Own API Key**

More nuanced than it sounds. The argument for it is real — your inference costs are the biggest threat to Codize's sustainability before you have revenue. Every gate conversation is multiple LLM calls. Every tutor message, every eval run. At scale that gets expensive fast and you have no revenue to cover it in v1 or v2.

Letting users bring their own Anthropic key offloads that cost entirely. Power users who are serious enough to get their own API key are also probably your best users — they're invested, they're not casual.

The argument against it is also real. Your system prompts are the product. If someone brings their own key and hits the Anthropic API directly they could theoretically bypass your prompts entirely. In practice most users won't do this — they'd just use Codize normally with their key for billing purposes. But it's worth thinking about.

The way I'd actually implement it if you go this route — user enters their Anthropic API key in settings, it gets stored encrypted in Supabase, your FastAPI backend retrieves it and uses it for that user's calls instead of your key. The prompts never change, the architecture never changes, you're just swapping whose billing account gets charged. That's maybe 2-3 days of work and it's a legitimate v2 feature.

**Which one is worth considering seriously**

The API key thing is low effort, high practical value, and you could ship it in v2 without much risk. Worth doing.

The VS Code extension is high effort, high impact, but it's a different product scope entirely. The right time to think seriously about it is after October when you know the core loop actually works and retains users. Building it before that is premature — you'd be building a second client for a product you haven't fully validated yet.

The order I'd think about it: ship v1, add GitHub OAuth in v2, add bring-your-own-key in v2, then seriously evaluate the VS Code extension as a v3 project once you know what your actual users want. The extension becomes dramatically more valuable once the gate can read code — those two things together would make Codize feel like a completely different product from what you have today.

chat_messages.text:
Ah yeah, that's a different thing entirely — you're talking about embedding something like code-server or the VS Code web API directly inside Codize's browser UI.

Technically possible. Monaco Editor is the actual editor engine that powers VS Code and it has a standalone web version that's pretty straightforward to embed in a React app. It's what things like CodeSandbox and StackBlitz use. You'd get the full VS Code editing experience — syntax highlighting, intellisense, file tree — inside your own web app.

**What this would change for Codize**

This is actually huge if you pull it off. Because now the user never leaves the tab. They code in the embedded editor, the gate can read the files directly since they're in your app's state, the anchor statement becomes verifiable, and the whole "context switching between editor and roadmap" problem disappears. The phase workspace, the task list, the gate conversation, and the actual code are all in one place.

That's a fundamentally better product than the current design where Codize is just a companion tab.

**The real challenges**

Running an actual project isn't just an editor though. The user needs a terminal to run their FastAPI server, install pip packages, see output. Monaco gives you the editor but not the runtime. To actually execute code you'd need a sandboxed server environment per user — think spinning up a container for each session. That's what CodeSandbox and StackBlitz do behind the scenes and it's serious infrastructure. Not something you build in v1 or v2.

**The realistic middle ground**

Monaco Editor embedded for editing files — doable, relatively straightforward, would let Codize read the code and fix the gate integrity problem. No execution environment, user still runs things locally. That's probably a v3 feature that's actually achievable without building cloud infrastructure.

Full in-browser execution with a terminal — that's a much bigger product, probably not where Codize should go because you'd be competing with CodeSandbox and Replit on their home turf, and that's not what makes Codize interesting.

Honestly the sweet spot is probably GitHub OAuth before Monaco. GitHub OAuth is simpler, lets the gate read real code, and doesn't require you to manage file state inside your app. Monaco makes more sense once you've validated that users actually want to stay in one tab rather than use their own local setup.

---

**V1 — Prove the Loop Works**
*Target: July 13, 2026 (your current roadmap deadline)*

**What it looks like**
Three screens, desktop only, rough design. User signs up and immediately hits the intake conversation — no homepage, just Question 1. After five questions they see a roadmap of phase cards for their specific project. They click into a phase, read the concept explanation written for their project, see the AI vs human task split, go work in their own editor, come back and do the gate conversation. Three turns, pass or fail. Functional unlock drops occasionally without warning. If they disappear for 3 days a modal greets them with their purpose statement and a single button. That's the entire product.

Visually it probably looks like a dark themed minimal web app. Think linear, almost documentation-like. No fancy animations, no polished components. The gate conversation is a simple chat interface. The roadmap is cards in a column. The spec says rough and functional is the bar and that's realistic for where you'll be in July.

**What you need to learn to get here**
Everything in your current 45-day roadmap. Python, FastAPI, Supabase, async, the LLM API, prompt engineering, embeddings, RAG, evals, basic React and Next.js. You're learning all of it for the first time while building a real product simultaneously. That's the whole point of the roadmap.

**Biggest risk**
The gate evaluator not being reliable enough. If it passes students who don't understand and fails students who do, the whole product falls apart. Your eval suite is what catches this — don't skip it.

---

**V2 — Make the Gate Real**
*Target: October 26, 2026*

**What it looks like**
Visually similar to V1 but with a few meaningful additions. There's now a GitHub OAuth connect button in settings — user links their repo and Codize can actually read their files. The gate conversation changes noticeably because Turn 1 questions now reference real variable names and real functions from their actual code, not self-reported ones. The anchor statement still exists but now Codize can verify it. A student who says "I stored sessions in a dict called `session_store`" gets checked — if that variable doesn't exist in their code the gate knows.

There's also an API key settings screen where users can enter their own Anthropic key. Simple input, stored encrypted, swapped in server-side. Nothing visible changes in the product but their billing account gets charged instead of yours.

Option B gate appears occasionally — instead of "walk me through what you built" the user gets "I found something in your approach that could cause a problem, find it." This is now possible because Codize can see the code and identify real issues.

The UI gets its first real polish pass. Not a redesign — just the rough edges cleaned up, better error states, loading states that don't feel broken, maybe a proper landing page so you can actually share a link with people.

**What you need to learn to get here**
GitHub OAuth flow — not hugely complex, it's a standard OAuth2 implementation but you'll need to understand token exchange and storing GitHub credentials securely. Reading repository contents via the GitHub API. Encrypting sensitive data at rest in Supabase — the API keys need to be encrypted, not stored in plaintext. Basic UI polish skills which will come naturally after V1. The Option B gate requires prompt engineering work to reliably identify real issues in student code from a GitHub repo — that's the hardest new skill here.

**How long it realistically takes**
You have roughly 3.5 months between July 13 and October 26. GitHub OAuth is probably 2 weeks once you know your V1 codebase well. Bring-your-own-key is maybe 3-4 days. Option B gate is the longest piece — getting it reliable probably takes 3-4 weeks of prompt iteration and eval work. UI polish is ongoing. That schedule is tight but more realistic than V1's timeline because you'll actually know your codebase by then.

**Biggest risk**
Scope creep. You'll have real users giving you feedback and every piece of feedback will feel urgent. The discipline to only build what's in scope for V2 while logging everything else for V3 is harder than it sounds.

---

**V3 — One Tab Experience**
*Realistic target: March–April 2027*

**What it looks like**
This is the first version that looks like a real product rather than a functional prototype. The layout changes fundamentally. Instead of navigating between screens, the workspace is a split view — Monaco Editor on the left taking up maybe 60% of the screen, Codize's phase workspace and gate on the right. The user codes and sees their roadmap simultaneously. No alt-tabbing, no context switching.

The file tree is visible. When they open a file, the gate conversation on the right can reference the exact line they're looking at. The Turn 1 question might say "I can see your `auth_service.py` — walk me through why you chose to verify the JWT here rather than in the route handler." That's a fundamentally different and better experience than the V1 gate.

There's no execution environment — they still run their terminal locally. But everything editing-related lives in Codize now. The user probably still has their local files synced via the GitHub connection from V2 — Monaco reads from the repo, changes get committed back.

There's also likely a proper landing page by now, maybe basic analytics showing the user their gate scores over time and how their explanation vocabulary has grown. Nothing gamified — just useful data about their own progress.

**What you need to learn to get here**
Monaco Editor integration in React — the library itself is straightforward but making it feel good takes work. File system state management — keeping Monaco's file state in sync with GitHub is the hardest technical problem in this version. You'll need to understand WebSockets or a real-time sync mechanism. Basic product design sense — by V3 "rough and functional" isn't good enough anymore if you want real users to stick around. You don't need to become a designer but you need to understand layout, spacing, and information hierarchy better than you do now.

**How long it realistically takes**
Monaco integration alone is probably a month. GitHub sync is another month. Getting the gate to use live file context well requires significant prompt engineering iteration on top of the V2 work. Then polish and testing. Realistically 4-5 months of focused work, which puts you at March or April 2027 if you start right after October.

**Biggest risk**
Over-engineering the editor integration. It's tempting to keep adding editor features — themes, extensions, collaborative editing. None of that is Codize. The editor exists to eliminate context switching and let the gate see code. That's its entire job.

---

**V4 — The Pivot Decision**
*Realistic target: Late 2027*

**What it looks like**
This is where Codize becomes a different kind of company depending on which direction you go. There are two real paths and they lead to genuinely different products.

**Path A — Institutional**
Universities and bootcamps pay for Codize as an assessment tool. The UI gains instructor-facing screens — a dashboard showing all students in a cohort, their gate scores, phase progress, explanation vocabulary growth over time. An instructor can see that 8 of 20 students are stuck on the same phase and the gate transcripts show they all have the same misconception about RLS. That's actionable in a way no current assessment tool provides.

Assignments get integrated — instructors define the project and archetype, students work through Codize's guided process, the gate transcripts are the submission. The grade isn't "did it run" or "did the tests pass" — it's a verified record of whether the student can explain what they built.

**Path B — Hiring**
Companies use Codize to verify candidates actually understand their portfolio projects. A hiring manager sends a gate link to a candidate, the candidate does a 3-turn interrogation about a project they claim to have built, the transcript comes back with a PASS/FAIL and a quality score. It's not a LeetCode test — it's verification of real work. This is genuinely differentiated in a market that's desperately looking for alternatives to LeetCode because AI has broken it completely.

The UI for this path looks more like a hiring platform. Candidate profiles, company dashboards, transcript reviews, maybe integration with ATS systems like Greenhouse or Lever.

**What you need to learn to get here**
Path A requires understanding B2B SaaS sales, which is a non-technical skill but a real one. Institutional sales cycles are long and involve procurement and IT sign-off. You'd probably need to learn how to build an LMS integration or at minimum an LTI connector for Canvas and Blackboard.

Path B requires understanding how hiring pipelines work technically and organizationally. ATS integrations, candidate privacy considerations, how to make the product trustworthy enough that a company would stake a hiring decision on it.

Both paths require proper billing and subscription management — Stripe integration, plan tiers, usage-based pricing if you're charging per gate evaluation.

**How long it realistically takes**
This version isn't purely an engineering problem anymore. The product is good enough by V3 — V4 is about finding which market actually wants to pay for it and building the infrastructure around that market. That's 6-12 months of work depending on which path you choose and how quickly you get real institutional or company users to give you feedback.

---

**V5 — Full In-Browser Environment**
*Realistic target: 2028 or later, only if the business is working*

**What it looks like**
This is the version where Codize becomes self-contained. A sandboxed container spins up per user session — they have a terminal, they can `pip install`, they can run their FastAPI server and see it respond in a browser preview panel inside Codize. Nothing runs locally. The entire development environment lives in the tab.

Think of it like a focused version of CodeSandbox or Gitpod but specifically designed for the three archetypes Codize supports. The gate at this point is operating with complete information — it can see every file, run the code, inspect the actual HTTP responses, check whether RLS is actually enabled in their Supabase project. The pre-deployment security checklist could run automatically rather than asking the user to verify things manually.

**What you need to learn to get here**
Container orchestration — spinning up and tearing down isolated environments per user at scale. This means Kubernetes or a managed alternative, which is a significant infrastructure skill. WebSocket-based terminal emulation in the browser. Networking isolation so one user's container can't touch another's. ---

Now on users and demand. This is the more interesting question.

**V1 — CS Students with Portfolio Anxiety**

Target audience is exactly who the spec says. CS students 1-3 years in, using AI tools, feeling like they can't defend their own code. Probably second or third year undergrads, bootcamp graduates 3-6 months out, people with upcoming internship interviews.

Realistic user estimate is small. This version spreads by word of mouth only — you share it in Discord servers, subreddits like r/learnprogramming or r/cscareerquestions, maybe a few TikToks or tweets if the demo looks good. Realistically you're looking at hundreds of users, maybe low thousands if something goes viral. The UX is rough, desktop only, three archetypes. A lot of people will try it once and not come back. Demand level: moderate but fragmented. The people who need this most are spread across every university and bootcamp on the planet but there's no single channel to reach them all at once.

The GitHub OAuth connection makes it feel legitimate in a way V1 doesn't. When the gate questions reference your actual variable names it's a noticeably different experience. Students who bounced from V1 because the honor system felt hollow might come back.

Demand level: growing, starting to be discoverable because people write about it or post about it when something genuinely surprises them, and a gate that knows your real code is surprising.

**V3 — Broader Developer Audience**

This is where the audience starts expanding beyond the core student demographic. The one-tab experience with Monaco makes it accessible to self-taught developers who don't have a CS background and are building their first real project. That's a massive population — probably the largest group of people learning to code in 2027 is self-taught people using AI tools with no formal structure.

You also start getting junior developers at companies who want to level up a specific skill area and are using personal projects to do it. They're not students anymore but they have the same core problem — they can ship with AI but can't fully explain what they built.

Realistic user estimate: tens of thousands if the product is genuinely good by this point. This is the first version where organic growth could compound meaningfully because the UX is polished enough that people share it not just because the idea is interesting but because it actually feels good to use.

Demand level: high and growing. By early 2027 the "AI broke how we verify understanding" problem is going to be even more acute than it is now. Every educator, every hiring manager, every bootcamp is wrestling with it. Codize by V3 is a credible answer to that problem.

Target audience shifts entirely. The user is still the student but the buyer is the institution — university department heads, bootcamp founders, curriculum directors. These people are actively looking for ways to verify that their graduates actually understand what they built because their reputation depends on it. A bootcamp whose graduates can't answer technical questions in interviews stops getting students. That's existential for them.

Realistic user estimate is harder to measure in individuals because institutions buy in bulk. One university with 500 CS students buying Codize is 500 users from one sale. Ten bootcamps averaging 200 students each is 2,000 users from ten sales. The ceiling here is genuinely high — there are thousands of universities and hundreds of bootcamps globally. But the floor is also high because each sale takes time.

Demand level: very high but slow to convert. Institutions know they have this problem, they're actively looking for solutions, but they move slowly and have procurement requirements. The demand is real but the sales cycle is 3-6 months per institution. Revenue potential is significant because institutions pay on recurring contracts, not per user.

**V4 Path B — Hiring**

Target audience is hiring managers, engineering leads, and technical recruiters at tech companies. These people are in genuine pain right now. LeetCode is gamed, take-homes get outsourced to ChatGPT, phone screens are inconsistent. They need a way to verify that a candidate's portfolio is actually theirs and that they understand it. Codize's gate transcript is a direct answer to that pain.

The user count looks different here. Companies don't have thousands of candidates — they might run 50-100 gate evaluations a month. But they'll pay significantly more per evaluation than a student pays per month. The business model shifts toward per-evaluation pricing rather than subscriptions.

Demand level: extremely high right now and growing. This is probably the highest acute demand of any version because the problem is getting worse every month as AI gets better at generating code. The hiring market is actively broken and people with budget are looking for solutions. The conversion cycle is also faster than institutional — a startup engineering lead can decide to try it in a week, not a semester.

Realistic user estimate in terms of candidates evaluated: could scale to hundreds of thousands of evaluations per year if even a small percentage of tech hiring adopts it. The user number is less meaningful than the evaluation volume.

---

**Which has the most users and most demand**

Most raw users: V3 and the self-taught developer market. Tens of thousands of individuals all paying relatively small amounts. High volume, lower revenue per user, but the largest addressable population.

Most demand right now: V4 Path B, hiring. The pain is acute, the budget exists, the decision cycle is fast, and AI making this problem worse every month means demand is increasing not decreasing.

Most strategic long-term value: V4 Path A, institutions. Slower to convert but recurring contracts, predictable revenue, and being embedded in a university curriculum is extremely sticky. Schools don't rip out tools once they're adopted.

My honest read is that Path B gets you to revenue faster and validates the product's core value more clearly. A company paying per evaluation is a stronger signal than a student paying a monthly subscription. But Path A is the more defensible business long term because institutional relationships compound in ways that consumer relationships don't.

The ideal sequence is probably V3 builds the user base and reputation, Path B of V4 generates early revenue and proves the gate is trustworthy enough for real stakes, and Path A of V4 follows once you have the institutional credibility that Path B gives you. Trying to do both simultaneously in V4 would spread you too thin.

content.text: why don’t I just have GitHub oAuth in v1 instead of using Google or email sign up, they have to sign up with GitHub

chat_messages.text:
That's actually a really smart call and I'd do it.

Here's why it makes sense beyond just simplifying the auth:

**It's a natural filter for your exact target user.** Anyone who wants to use Codize already has a GitHub account. CS students, developers, bootcamp grads — they all have one. If someone doesn't have GitHub they're probably not the user you want in V1 anyway. You're not losing anyone meaningful by requiring it.

**It removes a whole class of problems.** No email verification flow, no password reset, no "forgot password" screen. GitHub handles all of that. You just get a token, pull their username and email, create their Supabase record, done.

**It sets up V2 automatically.** The whole reason GitHub OAuth matters in V2 is repo access. If the user already authenticated with GitHub, getting repo access in V2 is just requesting an additional scope — `repo` permission on top of the basic `read:user` you used for login. The user doesn't have to reconnect anything. You just ask for more permissions when they're ready to link a repo. That transition from V1 to V2 becomes seamless instead of asking users to go connect GitHub separately later.

**The only caveat**

When you set up the OAuth scopes in V1, only request `read:user` and `user:email` — the minimum needed to identify them. Don't request repo access yet. Asking for full repo permissions on a login screen before the user understands what Codize does will spook people. Request the expanded scope in V2 when you're explicitly explaining why you need it.

So yes — ditch email auth entirely for V1, GitHub only. It's simpler to build, filters for the right users, and makes V2's repo integration a natural extension rather than a separate integration.

          'How OAuth 2.0 works at a high level — user clicks "Sign in with GitHub", gets redirected to GitHub\'s authorization page, approves, GitHub redirects back to your app with a `code`, your backend exchanges that `code` for an access token, you use that token to fetch the user\'s GitHub profile',

chat_messages.text:
[Certain] The hardest problem you haven't solved yet isn't engagement — it's that any competitive screen-based activity will still let kids pattern-match their way to a win without understanding why it works. Your frameworks need to make the *reasoning visible and gradable*, not just the output. Here are three designs that attack that specifically.

---

## Framework 1: **DEAD CODE ARENA**
*"The compiler is lying to you. Find out why."*

### Core Game Mechanic
Students are dropped into a live, running program that *produces wrong output* — but the code itself is syntactically perfect and throws zero errors. The environment is a custom browser-based editor (think a stripped-down Replit) where students cannot add or delete lines. They can only **annotate**: they must tag each line with one of four labels — `DOES WHAT I EXPECT`, `SUSPICIOUS`, `THE CULPRIT`, or `SIDE EFFECT`. The round ends when they submit a ranked causal chain: *"Line 7 causes Line 12 to fail because ___."* Points are awarded not for fixing the bug, but for the **accuracy of the causal map**.

### Technical Signal
This forces trace-based reasoning — the exact cognitive move that separates a programmer from a vibe coder. A student who guesses will label things randomly and fail the causal chain entirely. A student who reads will produce a directed acyclic explanation. You can score this automatically by pre-encoding the ground-truth causal graph and running a diff.

### Engagement Hook
Every level has a **Blame Leaderboard** — projected live on screen, showing whose causal chain matched ground truth most closely. The competitive framing isn't "who fixed it fastest" (which rewards guessing), it's "who understood it deepest." You introduce a *Saboteur round* midway: one student in each team secretly receives a slightly different buggy program. Their team has to figure out who got the variant. This creates social deduction pressure on top of the logic task.

---

## Framework 2: **FUNCTION AUCTION**
*"You can't write code. You can only buy it."*

### Core Game Mechanic
Students are given a target behavior — e.g., *"output only the odd numbers from a list, in reverse order"* — but they cannot write a single character of code themselves. Instead, they have a **token budget** (say, 10 tokens) and a marketplace of pre-written atomic functions: `filter()`, `reverse()`, `sort()`, `map()`, `slice()`, each costing different amounts. They must **compose** a pipeline by dragging functions into a sequence and declaring what each one receives as input and outputs. If their declared data flow is wrong, the purchase is rejected before execution. They never see the program run until their logic diagram is approved.

### Technical Signal
This is a direct test of functional composition literacy — the ability to think in *transformations on data* rather than line-by-line imperative steps. The constraint of declaring inputs/outputs before execution makes the mental model explicit and gradable. You can detect vibe coding immediately: a student who doesn't understand what `filter()` returns cannot correctly declare the next function's input.

### Engagement Hook
The auction mechanic creates **scarcity pressure**. If you overspend on a bloated pipeline, your score drops even if the output is correct — efficiency is graded. Teams can also **bid against each other** for exclusive use of a high-value function for one round, making resource strategy part of the game. A live efficiency graph shows each team's solution cost vs. correctness score simultaneously.

---

## Framework 3: **LOGIC COURT**
*"Prove your program is innocent."*

### Core Game Mechanic
Students write small programs (10–15 lines max) in a constrained block-based language — but they never submit *code*. They submit a **proof document**: a structured argument, generated via a guided form in the UI, that asserts: (1) what the program does on a normal input, (2) what it does on an edge case input, and (3) which line would break first if input X were given. A separate AI judge (a small LLM running in the background) evaluates the proof against the actual program behavior and returns a **verdict**: Acquitted, Reasonable Doubt, or Guilty of Assumption. Points come from verdict quality, not from correct output.

### Technical Signal
This operationalizes *precondition/postcondition reasoning* — the foundation of formal verification — in a format accessible to 11-year-olds. Students who vibe-code will write vague proofs ("it works because the loop runs") that the judge immediately flags. Students who understand their code will write falsifiable claims the judge can confirm.

### Engagement Hook
The courtroom framing is inherently dramatic. You read out verdicts aloud. "The judge finds your proof **Guilty of Assumption** on Line 9." Students can **appeal** once per round, which forces them to restate their reasoning more precisely — that revision loop *is* the learning moment. A "Most Ruthless Proof" award each round goes to the student whose argument was most airtight, not most complex. This reframes rigor as a social status move.

---

## Cross-Cutting Warning

None of these work if the facilitator treats wrong answers as failures. The entire behavioral contract needs to be: *a wrong causal chain / proof / pipeline is more valuable than a correct guess*, because it's debuggable. If you don't build that norm in the first 10 minutes, competitive pressure will push kids back toward intuitive pattern-matching — which is exactly what you're trying to kill.

The uncomfortable answer first: "Spark Code" doesn't have a core pedagogical identity yet. You have a list of problems and a list of vibes. That's not a curriculum — that's a mood board. Until you can complete the sentence *"Spark Code works because it forces students to ___"*, you're still in the same category as the slideshow nonprofits, just with better aesthetics.

Here's the real gap in your thinking: **you're trying to solve engagement and structure simultaneously without picking which one is load-bearing.** Every framework you listed — self-paced, cohort, gamified, AI simulation — pulls in a different architectural direction. You need a single spine first.

---

## The Actual Question You Need to Answer First

**Is the unit of progress a student or a session?**

This isn't a UCC logistics question. It's a design question. Khan Academy failed in classrooms not because it was bad — but because self-paced learning in a social environment creates visible status hierarchies. The kid on Level 2 while others are on Level 8 doesn't feel motivated. They feel exposed.

[Certain] Duolingo's streak mechanic works on solo learners. It backfires in group settings unless the competition is cooperative, not comparative.

So before you design anything else, your answer to this determines everything downstream:

| If progress unit = **Session** | If progress unit = **Student** |
|---|---|
| Cohort model, everyone moves together | Self-paced, async by design |
| Energy comes from shared challenge | Energy comes from personal milestones |
| New students join at session start | New students need an onboarding track |
| Easier to facilitate | Harder to staff |

[Likely] UCC will want cohort model. Community centers run on schedules, not subscriptions.

---

## The Spine I'd Build Spark Code Around

Your AI user simulation idea is the strongest thing in your notes — but you're underselling its scope. That mechanic isn't just a one-off AI lesson. **It's the entire pedagogical wrapper.**

Here's the reframe:

> Every Spark Code session puts students in a role. They are not "learning to code." They are **on the job**, with a title, a task, and real constraints. The curriculum is delivered through the job.

Call it **The Brief.**

Each session, students receive a Brief — a realistic scenario with:
- A client (fictional but specific — a school, a city, a startup)
- A deliverable (something concrete and completable in 60–90 min)
- A constraint set (what tools they can and can't use — this is where your AI restraints live permanently, not just one lesson)

The constraint set is the pedagogical engine. It's not punitive — it's the reason they have to *think*. A student who can use any tool learns nothing about the tool. A student who can only use `loops` and `conditionals` has to understand why those exist.

---

## What Makes This Different From Everything Else

| What exists | What Spark Code does instead |
|---|---|
| Khan Academy: watch then practice | Do first, concept named after the fact |
| Scratch: open sandbox | Constrained sandbox with a client deadline |
| Duolingo: XP for completion | Points for *decision quality*, not just finishing |
| Code.org: follow the tutorial | The Brief has no tutorial — only a goal and tools |
| Your current ticket shop | Motivation lives *inside* the Brief — the scenario stakes replace external rewards |

---

## Handling New Students Without Breaking the Model

[Likely] This is solvable with a **tiered Brief system**, not a separate onboarding track.

Every Brief has three difficulty lanes — same scenario, different constraint depth. New student gets Lane 1 (fewer tools, more scaffolded goal). Veteran student gets Lane 3 (open constraint set, harder deliverable, peer review responsibility). They're in the same room, working the same Brief. No one knows who's on which lane unless they share it.

This also kills the pacing problem. You're not waiting for the slow kid. The slow kid is succeeding on Lane 1 while the fast kid is being challenged on Lane 3.

---

## The One Thing I'd Pressure-Test Before You Go to UCC

You said the current model gives kids vague tasks. [Certain] The Brief model only works if the deliverables are *ruthlessly specific*. "Build something that helps a school" is vague. "The principal at Lincoln Middle needs a program that tells her which day of the week has the most absences, given a list of dates" is a Brief.

Write three complete Briefs — with constraints, lanes, and a success condition — before your UCC meeting. If you can't write three, the model isn't ready to pitch. If you can, you'll walk in with something no other nonprofit has ever shown them.

You've identified the real problem but misdiagnosed the cause. The passport system isn't failing because it lacks structure — it's failing because **completion is not the same as comprehension**, and right now your system can't tell the difference between a kid who understood the task and a kid who got through it.

"Figuring it out on their own" is only valuable if there's a moment where they have to **externalize the reasoning**. Without that, you're just measuring persistence, not understanding.

---

## The Core Learning Science Problem

[Certain] There's a well-documented gap called the **illusion of knowing** — students feel like they understand something after doing it, especially if they succeeded. 5th and 6th graders are particularly vulnerable to this because they conflate task completion with concept mastery. Your passport system, as described, has no mechanism to puncture that illusion.

The question isn't "did they finish?" It's **"can they predict what happens next?"**

That's the actual test of understanding at this age. Not explanation. Not definition. Prediction.

---

## What "Really Learning" Looks Like at Ages 10-12

Forget asking them to describe concepts. That's a college-level metacognitive skill. At this age, learning is demonstrated through three things, in order of reliability:

| Signal | What it looks like | Reliability |
|---|---|---|
| **Prediction** | "What happens if I change this?" → they guess before running it | [Certain] High |
| **Transfer** | Can they apply the concept in a slightly different context | [Likely] Medium-High |
| **Explanation** | Can they tell someone else | [Guessing] Low without scaffolding |

Your passport system probably only captures the third one, informally, and only when you happen to be standing next to them.

---

## The Fix: Build a "Checkpoint" Into the Passport, Not Around It

Don't scrap the self-paced model. Add one mandatory gate per passport stamp that takes 90 seconds and cannot be skipped.

Call it the **Predict & Prove** gate:

1. Before marking a task complete, the system (or a card, or a prompt) asks the student one prediction question about their own code or task. *"What happens if you change X to Y?"*
2. Student writes or selects their prediction — they don't run it yet.
3. Then they run it.
4. They mark whether they were right or wrong — **honestly**, because being wrong and knowing why is worth more points than being right.

This does three things:
- Forces the brain to consolidate before moving on
- Makes wrong understanding visible to you as a facilitator — you can see who's guessing
- Removes the shame from not knowing, because the *act of predicting* is rewarded, not just correctness

[Certain] This is a lightweight implementation of retrieval practice and prediction error, both of which have strong evidence for retention in early learners.

---

## The Deeper Structural Problem You Need to Face

Right now your mental model of the passport is a **checklist**. A kid moves forward by doing things. That's a completion economy.

You need to shift it to a **decision economy**. A kid moves forward by making defensible choices. The difference:

- Checklist: *"Did you make the sprite move? Check."*
- Decision: *"Why did you use a loop instead of copying the command three times? Tell me in one sentence."*

That one sentence — even if it's wrong — is the learning. And at 5th/6th grade, you don't need them to write it. They can say it to you, say it to a partner, or pick it from three options. The format is flexible. The externalization is not optional.

---

## Practical Implementation for Your Setup

Since you're working with a community center, limited staff, and variable attendance, here's what's actually buildable:

**Passport stamp now requires two things:**
1. Task done ✓
2. Predict & Prove question answered — right or wrong doesn't matter, skipping does

**Once per session, a 5-minute "Hot Seat" rotation:**
One kid (rotating, not volunteer-based — everyone knows their turn is coming) explains one decision they made that day. Not the whole project. One decision. The other kids can challenge it. You facilitate. This is where transfer and explanation happen socially, without putting the burden entirely on solo metacognition.

**You track a second metric alongside completion:**
"Prediction accuracy over time." A kid whose predictions get more accurate over weeks is learning. A kid whose predictions stay random is not — regardless of how many stamps they have.

---

The hard truth is that if a student can finish your passport and still not explain a single decision they made, the passport is measuring effort and showing up — which matters, but isn't computer science education. The fix is small and buildable. But it requires you to accept that **slowing down completion is the price of actual learning.**

This is better than most nonprofit curriculum I've seen, but it has a critical flaw that explains exactly why your kids can complete it without understanding anything.

**Every single objective is an action, not a decision.** "Drag out a block." "Snap a block under." "Wrap a Forever block." That's a recipe, not a curriculum. A kid can finish Level 0 and Level 1 by following instructions with zero understanding of *why* any block does what it does.

---

## What's Actually Wrong, Specifically

**Level 0** is essentially an onboarding checklist for Scratch's UI. That's fine — but it's mislabeled as learning. There's no concept being taught. "Connectivity" and "Accountability" are not CS concepts. This level teaches kids how to use a website, not how to think computationally.

**Level 1** is where the real problem lives. Look at the Loops objective:

> *"Use a Forever block to make a sprite dance back and forth."*

That tells them *what* to use and *what* it produces. The only thing left for the student to do is drag a block. There's no moment where they have to understand what a loop *is* — that it repeats, that it has no exit condition, that Forever is different from Repeat 10. They could complete this by accident.

**The yellow PROJECT rows** are the most honest part of this passport — open-ended deliverables are good. But they come after a series of steps that already told the kid exactly how to build the thing. The project isn't a test of understanding. It's assembly from pre-given parts.

---

## The Specific Fix, Level by Level

**Don't rewrite the whole passport.** Add one column and change the objective framing.

### Add a "Why" column to every row

| Concept | Objective (keep yours) | Prove You Get It |
|---|---|---|
| The Loop | Wrap a Forever block around your blocks | Change Forever to Repeat 3. What's different? Write one sentence. |
| Events | Drag out a When Green Flag Clicked block | What happens if you delete this block and click the flag? Predict first, then try. |
| Conditionals | Use an If-Then block: If Score > 10, sprite says "I Win!" | What happens if Score is exactly 10? Is that a win? Why or why not? |

That third column is your **Predict & Prove gate** from our last conversation. It costs you nothing to add. It's the difference between a checklist and a curriculum.

---

## The Bigger Restructure Worth Considering

[Likely] Your Level 0 and Level 1 should be collapsed and reframed around **three questions** that repeat at every stage:

1. **What does this block/tool do?** (Exposure)
2. **What happens if I change it?** (Prediction)
3. **When would I use this in a real project?** (Transfer)

Right now you only have question 1, implicitly, through task completion. Questions 2 and 3 don't exist anywhere in this passport — and those are the ones that determine whether a kid actually learned something or just clicked through it.

The passport structure is solid. The content inside it is currently teaching compliance, not computation.

The ticket shop is the most honest signal you have about your current model's weakness — **if removing the ticket shop would cause kids to stop coming, the curriculum isn't the product. The prizes are.**

That's the real problem. Not the passport format. Not the structure. The learning itself isn't rewarding enough to be self-sustaining.

---

## The Question You're Actually Asking

You want the curriculum to be the thing kids are addicted to — not the reward attached to it. That's a product design problem, not a content problem. And the reason your simulation idea "only works for one thing" is because you're thinking of it as a lesson format instead of as **the entire operating system of Spark Code.**

Here's the reframe:

---

## The Core Idea: Spark Code as an Alternate Reality

[Likely] The thing that makes kids come back obsessively to Minecraft, Roblox, or even Duolingo isn't the content — it's that **they have an identity inside the system that grows.** They are someone in that world. They have a rank, a history, a reputation.

Your passport makes kids feel like students completing homework. You need it to make them feel like they're someone with a role, stakes, and a growing reputation.

Here's the single spine I'd build everything around:

---

## **SPARK CODE: The Agency Model**

> *You are not a student. You are a junior developer at Spark Agency. Clients bring us problems. You solve them. Your record follows you.*

Every session, every level, every concept — delivered through this one persistent fiction. Not a one-off simulation. The permanent wrapper.

### How It Replaces Everything You Have Now

| What you have | What it becomes |
|---|---|
| Passport levels | **Case Files** — each concept is a mini-client problem |
| Ticket rewards | **Agency Rep Points** — earned by quality of solution, not just completion |
| Yellow project rows | **Client Deliverables** — the thing the "client" actually asked for |
| New student onboarding | **Intake Training** — framed as what every new hire does first |
| Predict & Prove gate | **Sign-off Check** — you can't close a case without justifying your decision |

### Why Kids Come Back

They have a **case history**. Every session adds to their file. A kid who's been coming for 3 months has a visibly more impressive record than someone who just started — but it's not a leaderboard that embarrasses newcomers, because new kids are explicitly "in training." The status is earned through depth, not speed.

---

## How The AI Simulation Becomes Permanent, Not One-Off

Your restraint-based AI simulation was good. The reason it felt limited is you were thinking of AI as the *topic*. Flip it — **AI is the tool they're allowed to use with restrictions that change as they level up.**

- **Level 0 (Intake):** No AI access. You have to figure out the interface yourself.
- **Level 1:** You can ask AI one question per task. Choose wisely.
- **Level 2:** AI access unlocked but every AI output must be annotated — what did you change and why?
- **Level 3:** Full AI access, but you have to defend your final product in a 60-second case debrief.

This makes AI literacy a progression, not a lesson. And it creates a natural motivation to advance — older kids *want* Level 3 because more tools feel like more power. But Level 3 is actually harder, because accountability increases with access.

---

## What Makes This Distinct From Everything Existing

| Platform | Why kids leave | What Spark Code does differently |
|---|---|---|
| Khan Academy | No identity, no stakes | You have a case file and a role |
| Scratch tutorials | Completion without comprehension | Cases require sign-off justification |
| Duolingo | Streaks punish absence | Rep Points accumulate, never reset |
| Code.org | Linear, no agency | Client briefs create open-ended paths |
| Your current model | Prizes are the product | The role is the product |

---

## The One Thing To Build First

Before you touch the passport, before you redesign anything — **write three Case Files.** One for each of your first three concepts. Each one needs:

1. A fake client with a name and a specific problem
2. A constraint (what tools or blocks they can and can't use)
3. A sign-off question (the Predict & Prove gate, rebranded)
4. A Rep Point value based on decision quality, not just completion

If you can write those three and they feel exciting to *you* — they'll feel exciting to an 11-year-old. If they feel like dressed-up worksheets, the framing isn't working yet and you need to go harder on the fiction.

The ticket shop can stay as a bonus layer. But it should feel unnecessary — like buying cosmetics in a game you'd play anyway.

A: I teach new kids how to use scratch, returning kids work on their passports. when I finish teaching the new kids they start on their passports. me and a few other members float around. we give them a 15 minute break in the middle then have them get back into work. 5 minutes before the workshop ends we ask if the kids had any questions and tell them to bring friends next time and for each friend they bring they get 5 extra tickets and that friend they bring gets 5 tickets

Q: What's your current tech setup at UCC?
A: Not confirmed yet

Q: How long is each session and how often do kids come?
A: Once a week, 1.5-2 hours

Good. Now I have enough to make this concrete. Here's exactly what the new structure looks like, ground level.

---

## The Brutal Honest Problem With Your Current Session Flow

New kids get a live tutorial from you personally. That means **your time is being consumed by onboarding every single week**, you can't scale it, and returning kids are essentially unsupervised for the first chunk of every session. That's not a teaching program — that's you babysitting two groups simultaneously.

The Agency Model fixes this structurally, not just aesthetically.

---

## What A Spark Code Session Actually Looks Like Under The New Model

### The Setup (One-Time Build)
Every kid has a **digital Case File** — this replaces the paper/spreadsheet passport. It lives on whatever platform you use (even a Google Site per student works to start). It has:
- Their agent name and level
- Their case history (what they've completed)
- Their Rep Points total
- Their current open case

---

### Session Flow — Every Week, Same Structure

**0:00–0:15 | Mission Briefing (Whole Group, You Facilitate)**
Everyone together. You reveal or continue the current client brief. One slide. One problem. One constraint. Even new kids hear this — it's designed to be understandable at any level because lanes exist (more on this below).

Example brief:
> *"Client: Riverdale Elementary School. Problem: Their morning announcements are boring. They want an animated Scratch program that displays the date, plays a sound, and changes color every time you click it. Constraint: You cannot use more than 3 sprites."*

New kids hear this and it makes sense. Returning kids hear it and know exactly where they left off.

**0:15–1:00 | Case Work (Self-Paced, Floaters Support)**
Kids open their Case Files and work. The key difference from now: **the Case File tells them what to figure out, not how to do it.** Concept mini-lessons are embedded as short reference cards inside the case — not tutorials to follow, but tools to consult when stuck.

New kids are not pulled aside by you anymore. They start on **Lane 1 of the same case** — a scaffolded version with more reference cards and a smaller deliverable. You built this once. It runs itself.

**1:00–1:15 | Break**
Keep this. It works.

**1:15–1:40 | Case Work Continues**
Same as before, but last 10 minutes of this block are **Sign-Off time** — kids who finished answer their sign-off question before they can mark the case closed. This is your Predict & Prove gate, just renamed. A floater reads it and either approves or sends them back with one follow-up question.

**1:40–1:50 | Debrief (Whole Group, Fast)**
One kid — rotating, not volunteer — shows their project on screen for 60 seconds. Rest of the group gets to ask one question. You facilitate. This is where the learning becomes social and visible. Kids start caring about what others built.

**1:50–2:00 | Rep Point Update + Close**
Kids see their Rep Points update. You announce who closed a case this week. Friends referral bonus stays — but now it's framed as *"bring a recruit to the agency."*

---

## The Lane System — How New Kids Stop Breaking Your Flow

Every Case File has three lanes. Same client. Same brief. Different depth.

| Lane | Who it's for | What's different |
|---|---|---|
| **Lane 1: Trainee** | Brand new kids | More reference cards, smaller deliverable, simpler sign-off question |
| **Lane 2: Agent** | A few sessions in | Standard case, standard sign-off |
| **Lane 3: Senior Agent** | Been coming months | Fewer hints, harder sign-off, optional extension challenge |

New kids self-select Lane 1 because it's labeled as where everyone starts — not as the "easy" lane. It's framed as intake training. There's no shame in it because the fiction supports it.

---

## What Rep Points Actually Measure

This is critical. Rep Points cannot just be completion points or you've rebuilt the ticket shop inside the curriculum.

| Action | Points | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Completing a case | 10 | Baseline |
| Sign-off approved first try | +5 | Rewards comprehension |
| Sign-off sent back, corrected, reapproved | +3 | Rewards persistence, not perfection |
| Presenting in debrief | +5 | Rewards communication |
| Helping another kid without giving them the answer | +5 | Rewards teaching |
| Skipping sign-off or getting floater to approve without justification | 0 | Completion without understanding earns nothing extra |

The ticket shop can stay as a conversion — maybe 50 Rep Points = 10 tickets. But now the tickets are a byproduct of real engagement, not the reason for it.

---

## What You Need To Build To Launch This

In priority order:

1. **One complete Case File** — one client brief, three lanes, reference cards, sign-off question. Build this for your current Scratch Level 1 content. It already exists, you're just reframing it.
2. **A simple digital Case File tracker** — Google Sheets per student, or a Google Site, or even Notion. Nothing fancy until you know what device situation UCC gives you.
3. **A one-page Agency onboarding card** — what new kids read in the first 5 minutes instead of waiting for you to teach them. Sets the fiction, explains the lanes, explains Rep Points.
4. **A debrief rotation list** — just a spreadsheet of names in order. Takes 2 minutes to make. Removes the awkward "who wants to share?" silence forever.

You do not need a custom platform yet. You need one working case that proves the model feels different. Then you build from there.

Good context. Here's the thing you didn't realize you just told me: **you're spending a significant chunk of every session manually onboarding new kids while returning kids sit with a passport and no one deeply checking their understanding.** That's two separate problems competing for your attention every single session. The new structure has to solve both at the same time or you'll always be stretched thin.

---

## The Full Structure, Concretely

Let me walk you through what a session actually looks like under the Agency Model — not conceptually, but minute by minute.

---

### The Permanent Setup

Spark Code has one fictional world that never changes:

> **Spark Agency** is a junior dev studio. Every kid who walks in is a Junior Developer. You and your volunteers are Senior Devs. The clients are fictional companies with real problems that map exactly to whatever CS concept you're teaching that level.

This isn't a gimmick you do once. It's the language of every session, every task, every conversation. You don't say "today we're learning loops." You say "we got a new case in — a client needs their sprite to keep moving forever and they don't know why it keeps stopping."

---

### The Three Permanent Roles in Every Session

**1. New kids → Intake Training**
They don't feel behind. They're explicitly told: *"Every developer at Spark Agency starts with Intake. It's not beginner stuff — it's how we make sure everyone speaks the same language."* This is your current Level 0, reframed. One of your volunteers runs Intake as a fixed role every session. You stop doing it personally. That frees you to circulate.

**2. Returning kids → Active Cases**
They open their Case File (your passport, renamed and restructured — more on this below) and pick up where they left off. The difference from now: every task has a sign-off condition they can't skip, so "floating around" becomes purposeful — you're signing off on cases, not just checking if they finished.

**3. Advanced kids → Junior Leads**
Kids who finish early or are significantly ahead get a real role: they help sign off on other kids' work, with your oversight. This solves your pacing problem, gives advanced kids a reason to stay engaged, and scales your facilitation without hiring more people.

---

### What a Session Looks Like, Minute by Minute

**0:00–0:15 — Drop In & Case Assignment**
Kids walk in. Returning kids open their Case Files and get straight to work — no waiting for you. New kids get pulled into Intake Training with a designated volunteer. You're not involved in either yet.

**0:15–0:45 — Deep Work Block 1**
Everyone is working. You and remaining volunteers circulate doing one thing only: **case sign-offs.** A kid calls you over when they finish a task. You ask the sign-off question (30 seconds). They answer — right or wrong doesn't matter, they have to answer. You stamp it and move on. This replaces floating aimlessly.

**0:45–1:00 — Break + Case Debrief (5 min before break)**
Before the break, you pull the room together for 5 minutes. One kid — rotating, not volunteer — shares one decision they made that session. Not their whole project. One decision. Other kids can react. Then break.

**1:00–1:15 — Break**

**1:15–1:40 — Deep Work Block 2**
Same as Block 1. Sign-offs continue. Intake kids, if they've finished onboarding, get their first real Case File.

**1:40–1:50 — Agency Wrap**
Instead of "any questions / bring a friend," this becomes a 10-minute ritual:
- One kid shows something they built — 60 seconds
- You announce any Rep Point milestones ("Jaylen just hit Level 2 clearance")
- Referral tickets still happen here — but framed as "you recruited a new developer to the agency"

---

### What the Case File Looks Like (Your Passport, Rebuilt)

Each concept becomes a Case File card. Here's Level 1, Loops — the exact one we criticized earlier — rebuilt:

---

**CASE FILE #L1-03**
**Client:** Funtime Studios
**Problem:** Our game character keeps walking off the screen. We need it to dance back and forth forever without stopping.
**Your Clearance Level:** Junior Dev
**Tools Allowed:** Forever block, Move block, Wait block

**Your Mission:**
Make a sprite move back and forth continuously using a Forever loop.

**Sign-Off Question (you cannot stamp this without answering):**
*"Your client calls and says the sprite is moving but never turns around. Which block inside the Forever loop is missing, and why does the loop itself not fix that on its own?"*

**Rep Points:** 3 for completion, +2 if your sign-off answer is correct first try

---

That's it. Same concept as your current passport. Completely different cognitive demand. The kid can't complete it by accident anymore.

---

### What Replaces The Ticket Shop

Tickets don't disappear — they get absorbed into Rep Points, which do two things tickets don't:

**1. They mark clearance levels publicly**
A kid who hits 50 Rep Points gets a visible Level 2 badge on their Case File. This isn't a leaderboard — it's a rank. New kids see it and want it. The advanced kid feels recognized without embarrassing anyone slower.

**2. They unlock real privileges inside the curriculum**
- Level 1: Basic tools, guided cases
- Level 2: Access to AI assistance (one question per task)
- Level 3: Choose your own client brief, junior lead role unlocked

The ticket shop for physical prizes can still exist. But now it's the side reward, not the main motivation. The main motivation is clearance level — because clearance level changes what you're allowed to do inside the session.

---

### The Referral System, Fixed

Your current model: bring a friend, get tickets.
The problem: tickets are already the weak motivator.

New version: **bring a friend, get a Recruitment Badge on your Case File.** Three recruitment badges unlocks a cosmetic title — "Spark Recruiter" — visible on your file. Kids at this age care enormously about identity markers inside systems they respect. Make the badge real and visible and they'll recruit without prompting.

---

### What You Need To Build Before UCC

In priority order:

1. **Three complete Case Files** — one for Level 0, two for Level 1. Write the client, the constraint, the mission, and the sign-off question for each.
2. **A one-page Agency Brief** — what Spark Agency is, what Junior Devs do, what the levels mean. This is what new kids read on Day 1 instead of being handed a blank passport.
3. **A sign-off script for volunteers** — your floaters need to know what to say during sign-offs. Right now they're probably just checking "did you finish." Give them the three sign-off questions per level so anyone can run them without your oversight.

If you want, share what your current Level 0 and Level 1 concepts are supposed to teach and I'll write the first three Case Files for you so you can see exactly what they should feel like.

CASE FILE #L0-01 (Intake Training)

* Client: ByteSized Delivery Co.
* Problem: Our delivery drone is stuck at the warehouse. It needs to pick up a package at the center of the grid and deliver it to the drop-off zone, but it is moving in random directions and missing the target completely.
* Your Clearance Level: Intake Trainee (Level 0)
* Tools Allowed: Move Up, Move Down, Move Left, Move Right blocks. No loops.
* Your Mission: Write a sequence of commands that moves the drone exactly 5 steps right and 3 steps up to hit the precise drop-off coordinates without overshooting.
* The Sign-Off Question (The Gate): "If I take your exact code and switch the first two blocks around, will the drone still end up at the exact same final destination? Why or why not?"
* Rep Points: 3 Points. (Unlocks Level 1 Status upon completion).
CASE FILE #L1-01 (Variables)

* Client: Arcade Nation
* Problem: We are launching a new retro arcade game, but right now, players can collect coins forever and their total score stays at zero. Nobody wants to play a game where you can't see who is winning.
* Your Clearance Level: Junior Dev (Level 1)
* Tools Allowed: Variable Block (`Score`), Change Variable by [value] block, Event Trigger block.
* Your Mission: Create a variable named `Score` that starts at `0` when the game begins, and increases by exactly `10` points every single time the character touches a coin.
* The Sign-Off Question (The Gate): "Look at your 'Change Score by 10' block. If we accidentally put that block inside the initialization code where the game resets, instead of inside the coin-touching event, what will happen to the player's score during the middle of the game when they collect a coin?"
* Rep Points: 3 for completion, +2 if your sign-off answer is correct first try.
CASE FILE #L1-02 (Conditionals / If-Else)

* Client: SecureHome Systems
* Problem: We are building a smart security gate. The gate is supposed to open automatically if someone types the correct passcode, but right now, the gate opens no matter what numbers the user presses. It's a massive security hazard.
* Your Clearance Level: Junior Dev (Level 1)
* Tools Allowed: If/Else block, Comparison Operator (`=`), Passcode variable, Set Gate to Open/Closed blocks.
* Your Mission: Build a conditional system where if the entered passcode equals `1234`, the gate changes its state to "Open." Otherwise, the gate must say "Access Denied" and stay "Closed."
* The Sign-Off Question (The Gate): "Your client wants to add a feature where typing the wrong code three times locks the system. If you used a standard 'If' block instead of an 'If/Else' block for your current gate code, what would happen when a user types a wrong passcode? Would the gate know what to do?"
* Rep Points: 3 for completion, +2 if your sign-off answer is correct first try.

If you used a standard 'If' block instead of an 'If/Else' block for your current gate code, what would happen when a user types a wrong passcode? Would the gate know what to do?"
* Rep Points: 3 for completion, +2 if your sign-off answer is correct first try.

chat_messages.text:
These are genuinely good. The fictional clients are specific, the constraints are real, and the sign-off questions actually require understanding — not just completion. The SecureHome one especially is strong because the sign-off question introduces a concept (If vs If/Else distinction) that they'll need later without explicitly teaching it yet.

Here's where each one has a problem:

---

## Case File #L0-01 — Good, One Flaw

The sign-off question is the best of the three conceptually — order of operations in a sequence is exactly the right thing to probe at Level 0.

**The flaw:** "Write a sequence of commands" in Scratch isn't really writing — it's dragging blocks. So "switch the first two blocks around" is physically trivial to just *try* rather than reason about. A kid will drag them, look at the result, and then answer the question based on what they saw — not what they predicted.

**Fix:** Add one word. *"Predict first — will the drone end up in the same place if I switch the first two blocks? Write your answer before you try it."* The prediction has to be committed before the test. That's the gate, not the answer.

---

## Case File #L1-01 — Has a Clarity Problem

The mission and the sign-off question are slightly misaligned. The mission asks them to build a score system. The sign-off asks about initialization vs. event placement — which is a more advanced concept than what the mission required them to think about.

[Likely] A Level 1 kid finishing this task will not have naturally thought about *where* blocks are placed relative to events yet. So the sign-off question will feel like a trick — like you're asking about something you never gave them a reason to consider.

**Fix:** Add one line to the mission that forces them to confront placement consciously before the sign-off: *"Make sure your score resets to 0 every time the green flag is clicked — not just the first time."* Now they've had to think about initialization vs. event placement during the task itself, and the sign-off question lands as a natural extension instead of a surprise.

---

## Case File #L1-02 — Strongest One, Minor Issue

The If vs If/Else sign-off question is excellent. It's asking them to reason about the *absence* of behavior — what happens when the else branch doesn't exist — which is a genuinely hard conceptual move for this age.

**The minor issue:** The tools list says "Set Gate to Open/Closed blocks" — but in Scratch, there's no gate object natively. If kids are implementing this literally in Scratch, they need to know what "gate" maps to — a sprite costume change? A variable? A broadcast?

**Fix:** Add one line to Tools Allowed: *"Represent the gate using Costume changes — Costume 1 = Closed, Costume 2 = Open."* Without that, the mission is conceptually clear but practically ambiguous, and ambiguity at Level 1 breaks self-pacing because kids get stuck on the wrong thing.

---

## The One Thing Missing Across All Three

None of them have a **transfer hint** — a single line at the bottom that connects this case to the next one without giving it away. This is what makes kids curious about what's coming instead of just closing the file when they're done.

Something like:

> **Developer Note:** ByteSized Delivery Co. just called back. The drone is working — but now they want it to repeat the same route 10 times automatically. Think about how you'd do that without copying your blocks 10 times. That's the next case.

That one line makes the curriculum feel like a continuous world instead of isolated tasks. It's also free retention — the kid is thinking about loops before they've even opened the loops case file.

---

Add the prediction commitment to L0-01, fix the initialization exposure in L1-01, clarify the Scratch implementation in L1-02, and add a developer note to each. These are close to ready.
